note: Updated Fri 9 Oct 2026, run before Asia's open; one normal session since Thursday 8 Oct's close. Thursday US close split sharply by duration: S&P 500 7,765.36 (-0.47%), Nasdaq Composite 27,193.34 (-1.25%, tech-led), Dow 51,231.64 (+0.10%, defensive/value resilience), Russell 2000 2,794.13 (+0.03%, an unusual divergence from its usual rate-sensitive-laggard role), VIX 15.41 (+2.19%, still a low-vol print despite risk-off headlines). Three genuinely new inputs this pass: (1) the Sept 15-16 FOMC minutes (released Oct 7, digested further Oct 8) showed all 19 officials backed the 25bp hike to 3.75-4.00%, with 16 of 18 projecting one more 2026 hike then a 2027 pause -- but market reaction was largely muted (equities/gold barely moved) since October-hike odds had already been cut to ~20% with JPMorgan favoring a December move instead; bitcoin was the one asset that sold off on the news (-1.72% to ~$81,845). (2) A weak 30-year Treasury auction (prior tail 5.31%/2.6bp) signals softer long-end demand, reinforcing the duration headwind alongside the confirmed hawkish dot plot. (3) Oil spiked on an escalating Hormuz tanker-attack campaign: a record 10 tankers were struck between Sept 28-Oct 4 (the highest weekly count on record) and strait crossings fell to a two-month low, driving Brent +3.58% to $103.79 and WTI +3.21% to $91.11. Gold (+0.57% to $4,164.30) and silver (-0.43% to $59.64) roughly stabilized as Hormuz-driven safe-haven demand partially offset the firm-dollar/elevated-real-yield headwind; gold remains ~23% below its January 2026 peak. Asia extended declines into Thursday's Wed/Thu closes (Nikkei -0.92%, KOSPI -1.98%, STI -1.63%, HSI -0.62%) on the same hawkish-Fed/oil backdrop. Weekly jobless claims ticked up modestly to 200k from 197k, consistent with gradual (not alarming) labor cooling. No active government shutdown -- the Sept 2 continuing resolution funds the government through Dec 11, 2026. China's rare-earth export-control truce (in place since the Oct 2025 Trump-Xi meeting) nears its Nov 10, 2026 expiry with no renewal signaled; coverage flags three live outcomes -- extension, selective reinstatement, or full reimposition of the Oct 2025 controls -- keeping the rare-earth basket a genuine binary-event trade over the next month.

macro.regime: Confirmed hawkish Fed meets a live Hormuz oil shock -- tech cracks, value/defensives hold, vol stays low
macro.narrative: The Fed's Sept 15-16 minutes confirmed a unanimous (19-0) hike to 3.75-4.00% under Chair Kevin Warsh, with 16 of 18 officials projecting one more 2026 hike before a 2027 pause; because October-hike odds had already fallen to roughly 20% ahead of the release, the broader equity and gold reaction was muted, but a weak 30-year Treasury auction (tail of 5.31%/2.6bp) is keeping long yields elevated and bitcoin sold off sharply as the one asset that reacted to the hawkish confirmation. Thursday's session showed clear duration bifurcation: the Nasdaq fell 1.25% on rate-sensitive tech while the Dow eked out a 0.10% gain and small caps were flat, a rotation into value/defensives rather than a broad risk-off move, and VIX at 15.41 still reflects low complacency. The dominant new driver is geopolitical: a record campaign of Iranian tanker attacks in the Strait of Hormuz (10 vessels struck between Sept 28-Oct 4, the highest weekly count on record) pushed strait crossings to a two-month low and sent Brent up 3.58% to $103.79 and WTI up 3.21% to $91.11, a stagflationary supply shock layered on top of an already-hawkish rate backdrop. Gold and silver stabilized (+0.57%/-0.43%) as safe-haven demand partially offset the firm-dollar/high-real-yield headwind, though gold remains about 23% below its January 2026 high. Labor data continues to cool only gradually (jobless claims 200k vs 197k prior), keeping the Fed on its hawkish path without forcing an early pivot, while fiscal risk stays contained with the government funded through Dec 11, 2026. China's rare-earth export-control truce nearing its Nov 10, 2026 expiry with no renewal signaled is the next binary catalyst on the calendar.
